subject: English
description: Passive voice — modal passives, perfect tenses, gerund passive, passive in questions/imperatives/with two objects.

questions.stem: Convert to passive: 'They will complete the project tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The project will be completed tomorrow
Project will completed by them now
The project completes by them tomorrow
Project shall complete tomorrow itself

questions.explanation: FUTURE SIMPLE PASSIVE: Subject + WILL/SHALL + BE + V3 (past participle) (+ by + agent). 'They will COMPLETE the project tomorrow' (active) → 'The project WILL BE COMPLETED tomorrow (by them)' (passive). 'By them' often dropped if agent is generic ('they'). PASSIVE VOICE FORMULAS for major tenses: (1) PRESENT SIMPLE: am/is/are + V3. 'She writes a letter' → 'A letter is written by her'. (2) PRESENT CONTINUOUS: am/is/are + being + V3. 'She is writing' → 'A letter is being written'. (3) PRESENT PERFECT: have/has + been + V3. 'She has written' → 'A letter has been written'. (4) PAST SIMPLE: was/were + V3. 'She wrote' → 'A letter was written'. (5) PAST CONTINUOUS: was/were + being + V3. (6) PAST PERFECT: had + been + V3. (7) FUTURE SIMPLE: will + be + V3. (8) FUTURE PERFECT: will + have + been + V3. KEY ELEMENTS: object of active becomes SUBJECT of passive; main verb becomes V3; appropriate FORM of 'BE' is added; original subject becomes 'by + agent' (often optional). PYQ FREQUENCY: passive voice tense conversions in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1-2× per cycle.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: 'Someone has stolen my bicycle.'

options.option_text: My bicycle has been stolen
My bicycle was stolen here also
My bicycle is stolen by someone
My bicycle stolen by someone there

questions.explanation: PRESENT PERFECT PASSIVE: HAS/HAVE + BEEN + V3. Active: 'Someone has STOLEN my bicycle' → Passive: 'My bicycle HAS BEEN STOLEN' (by someone — often dropped because 'someone' is unspecific). Tense PRESERVED: active is present perfect; passive must also be present perfect. KEY POINT: don't change the TENSE when converting voice. Each tense has its own passive structure. INDEFINITE AGENTS — 'BY' clause often DROPPED: when active subject is 'someone', 'people', 'they' (general) — passive often omits 'by ___' since it adds no info. EXAMPLES: (1) 'They speak English in Australia' → 'English is spoken in Australia' (drop 'by them'). (2) 'People built this temple in 1500 CE' → 'This temple was built in 1500 CE'. (3) 'Someone is knocking at the door' → 'The door is being knocked at'. PASSIVE WITHOUT AGENT is sometimes preferred when: (a) Agent is unknown. (b) Agent is obvious/unimportant. (c) Writer wants to FOCUS on the action/result, not the doer (common in scientific writing, news, official statements). PYQ FREQUENCY: voice transformations with present perfect in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per paper.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: 'The teacher must answer this question.'

options.option_text: This question must be answered
This question must answer here
This question must be answer there
Question must answered by teacher

questions.explanation: MODAL PASSIVE: MODAL + BE + V3. 'must answer' (active modal+verb) → 'must be answered' (passive). Common modals in passive constructions: CAN, COULD, MAY, MIGHT, MUST, SHOULD, OUGHT, WILL, WOULD. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + MODAL + BE + V3 (+ by + agent). EXAMPLES: (1) 'You must complete the form' → 'The form must be completed.' (2) 'They can solve this problem' → 'This problem can be solved.' (3) 'You should clean the room' → 'The room should be cleaned.' (4) 'She might write the report' → 'The report might be written.' MODAL PASSIVE MISTAKES: (a) Forgetting 'BE': 'must answered' (WRONG); needs 'must be answered'. (b) Wrong V3: 'must be answer' (WRONG); needs the past participle 'answered'. PRACTICE: convert these to passive — 'Workers should repair the road' → 'The road should be repaired.' 'They might cancel the match' → 'The match might be cancelled.' 'You can use this pen' → 'This pen can be used.' EXAM-FAVORITE: SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English error-spotting includes modal passive mistakes. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert to passive: 'They gave me a gift.'

options.option_text: I was given a gift (by them)
A gift was given me by them
Me was given by them a gift
By them I given a gift

questions.explanation: TWO-OBJECT VERBS (give, send, offer, lend, owe, pay, show, teach, tell, write) — when converted to passive, EITHER OBJECT can become the subject. Active: 'They gave ME a gift' (me = INDIRECT object; gift = DIRECT object). Passive Option 1 (preferred): 'I WAS GIVEN a gift (by them)' — indirect object becomes subject. Passive Option 2 (less common): 'A gift WAS GIVEN to me (by them)' — direct object as subject; note 'TO' before 'me' to maintain meaning. KEY DETAIL: in option 1, 'a gift' remains; in option 2, 'me' becomes 'to me' (preposition added). EXAM-FAVORITE: option 1 form (person becomes subject) is MORE COMMON in modern English. PRACTICE: (1) 'She told us a story' → 'We were told a story' OR 'A story was told to us'. (2) 'He sent her flowers' → 'She was sent flowers' OR 'Flowers were sent to her'. (3) 'They paid him 5000 rupees' → 'He was paid 5000 rupees' OR '5000 rupees were paid to him'. ANALOGY: 'GIVE' has 2 objects; 'me' is the recipient (indirect), 'gift' is the thing given (direct). Indirect-object-as-subject is preferred in passive. PYQ FREQUENCY: dative-object passives in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per paper.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: 'Open the door!' (imperative)

options.option_text: Let the door be opened
The door must open you here
Door is opened by someone there
Open the door is required now

questions.explanation: IMPERATIVE PASSIVE: typically uses 'LET + OBJECT + BE + V3'. Active: 'Open the door!' → Passive: 'LET THE DOOR BE OPENED.' Or alternatively: 'You are requested to open the door' (longer formal version). STRUCTURE: 'LET + OBJECT-AS-SUBJECT-OF-PASSIVE-CLAUSE + BE + V3'. EXAMPLES: (1) 'Close the window' → 'Let the window be closed'. (2) 'Solve this problem' → 'Let this problem be solved'. (3) 'Bring water' → 'Let water be brought'. (4) 'Don't disturb me' → 'Let me not be disturbed' OR 'I should not be disturbed'. NEGATIVE IMPERATIVES: 'Don't write on the wall' → 'Let the wall not be written on' OR 'You are not to write on the wall'. KEY ALTERNATIVES depending on tone: (a) 'You are advised/requested/ordered to + V1': formal. (b) 'Let + object + be + V3': standard imperative passive. (c) 'It is to be + V3': very formal. EXAM TIP: 'LET' construction is the EXAM-favorite for imperative passive — appears in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI English sections. INDIA exam contexts heavily test this construction. PYQ FREQUENCY: imperative-passive in SSC CGL Tier 2 voice-conversion section 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert to passive: 'Did the dog bite him?' (interrogative)

options.option_text: Was he bitten by the dog?
Was the dog bitten by him?
Did him be bitten by the dog?
Bites him by the dog?

questions.explanation: INTERROGATIVE (question) PASSIVE: maintain the same TENSE; rearrange so the OBJECT becomes SUBJECT, and the helping verb (auxiliary) precedes the new subject. Active: 'DID the dog BITE him?' (past simple interrogative). Passive: 'WAS he BITTEN by the dog?' (past simple passive interrogative). KEY METHOD: (1) Identify the active subject ('the dog'), object ('him'), main verb ('bite'). (2) Make the object the new subject ('he' subject form). (3) Use the appropriate passive structure for the same tense (past simple → was/were + V3). (4) For questions, AUXILIARY comes before SUBJECT. EXAMPLES: (a) 'Is she writing a letter?' → 'Is a letter being written by her?' (present continuous passive). (b) 'Have you finished the task?' → 'Has the task been finished by you?' (present perfect). (c) 'Will they invite us?' → 'Will we be invited by them?' (future simple). (d) 'Can you solve this?' → 'Can this be solved by you?' (modal). EXAM TRAP: students forget to convert pronouns: 'him' → 'he' (subject case); 'her' → 'she'; 'us' → 'we'; 'them' → 'they'. PYQ FREQUENCY: interrogative passives in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

questions.stem: Convert to passive: 'I remember meeting him.' (gerund)

options.option_text: I remember being met by him
He remembers meeting by me
I remember to be met by him
He is remembered by my meeting

questions.explanation: GERUND PASSIVE: convert 'meeting + object' (gerund as a -ing noun-form verb) to 'being + V3' (passive gerund). Active: 'I remember MEETING him' (gerund 'meeting' is the noun-form verb). Passive: 'I remember BEING MET by him.' Note: the SUBJECT 'I' stays SAME; only the gerund verb structure changes. STRUCTURE: passive gerund = 'being + V3' (also 'having been + V3' for perfect-passive gerund). EXAMPLES: (1) 'I love being praised' (passive gerund — 'someone praises me, and I love that'). (2) 'He hates being interrupted'. (3) 'She fears being noticed'. (4) 'Being told the truth was painful' (gerund as subject in passive form). PERFECT PASSIVE GERUND: 'having been + V3' = past completed action. 'Having been informed of the issue, she acted promptly'. KEY: gerunds are -ING verbs functioning as NOUNS. Passive gerunds describe the noun receiving an action. CONTRAST WITH INFINITIVE PASSIVE: 'to be + V3' — 'I want to be praised'. EXAM TRAP: don't confuse gerund passive 'being + V3' with present participle in continuous tense 'is being + V3'. PYQ FREQUENCY: gerund-passive constructions in CAT, IBPS PO Mains, RBI English — 1× per cycle.
